newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA DEBATES ACCIDENT FUND REFORM PROPOSALS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA DEBATES ACCIDENT FUND REFORM PROPOSALS.

text.p: South Africa's parliamentary transport committee and Motor Vehicle Accident Fund (MMF) officials met behind closed doors on Monday to debate a draft white paper on revamping the beleaguered fund.
But lobbyists said the proposal, known as the "draft white paper -- MK II", contained almost exactly the same proposals widely rejected by interested parties last year.
Lobby groups, some of which had sent representatives to the meeting from around the country at their own expense, and the media were barred from attending the meeting.
Committee chairwoman Patricia de Lille said they had been barred because the proposals were still in the "policy formation" phase.

A spokesman for the lobbyists claimed that the government was trying to push through the same proposals that were rejected last year by 75 interest groups. "This is not democratic or transparent," he said.
He said two lobby groups had sent letters to De Lille asking her to launch an urgent investigation into how chief executive Willem Swanepoel was running the fund.

The National Council for Quadriplegics in South Africa and the Drive Alive Trust said they were concerned that Swanepoel was ignoring instructions to take public views on the MMF into consideration and appeared to be pressing ahead with his own plans for the fund.
They accused him of making it increasingly difficult for injured or disabled accident victims to obtain compensation and said he was motivated "by a hidden agenda".

Funded through a 10 cents a litre levy on fuel, the MMF has been the subject of intense lobbying by lawyers, groups representing the disabled and road safety organisations for more than a year as government considers various ways of overhauling it.
Technically, the fund is insolvent and last year had a loss of more than seven billion rand if all pending claims had to be paid out straightaway.
In practice, however, the fund has assets of 1.25 billion rand and last year made a profit of 300 million rand.

Last year the government drafted a policy document or white paper that severely limited payments. Extensive public hearings were held and the white paper was more or less unanimously rejected. Legal drafters were told to start again, taking into accout the views expressed by the public.
One camp in government contends that the fund is too generous to accident victims and wants to place limits on payments.
Another camp believes that the fund is not paying out enough, especially to people disabled in road accidents.
De Lille said the planned white paper on the MMF would be released for public comment in two to three weeks time.
